No orphans: C-9, C-11, and C-13 each answer a job need stated in their own text — vocabulary fidelity, regression safety, and standing prose policy — and C-12's precedent requirement is anchored in the spec's own 'following the pattern already established for file-issue'. The seam is on criterion 2, and it is operational rather than nominal. Criterion 2 reads 'Each runs with and without the skill', which is a procedure. C-12 gets a method statement naming the delta into the preamble, and C-4 gets a stated baseline expectation into every scenario, but the only clause that requires an actual procedure is C-10, and C-10's procedure is defined as 'the steps that take a reader from a fixture name to a running scenario' — one run. Nothing requires that procedure to say how the no-skill run is performed, which for this skill is not obvious: it means a session where the skill is not loaded, against the same staged fixture, and the staging has to be repeated or the first run's deletions from `_inbox/` poison the second. That last point is not pedantic — process mode deletes from `_inbox/` (SKILL.md:130), so a reader who stages once and runs twice grades the baseline against an emptied inbox. | over-specification | minor | Answering the question you asked beyond pass or fail: yes, two clauses now carry machinery heavier than the failure they prevent, and the pattern is worth naming because it is what three rounds of audit produce if nobody stops it. C-7 is the clear case. It asks a checker to run a nine-row signal extraction against three inbox files, resolve each through a documented tiebreak, and separately verify a multi-project directory layout behind one non-textual signal. That is more procedure than the four other fixture clauses combined, for a deliverable that is a markdown table of expected tokens. The failure it prevents — a scenario expecting the wrong tier — is real, but the cheap version of the check catches it: 'read the inbox file, state which tier the reference's table and its narrowest-wins rule select, and compare to the expected token.' The row-by-row collection is what makes it feel rigorous and is not what makes it correct. If you keep the machinery, keep it because the tiebreak case genuinely needs it, and say so; do not add a fourth stage. C-10 is the milder case: four conjuncts where three do the work, and the one that does not ('writes nothing outside the scratch directory') is the one a checker has no instrument for. The broader observation, offered as the thing I would actually watch in Phase 2: eight of thirteen clauses now route to checker-judgment, and five of those require the checker to execute something — run a migrator, diff two trees, grep a fixture tree, run three smoke suites, load a rubric. A judgment checker that has to be right about a procedure before it can be right about a judgment fails in a way that reads as a bad verdict, and the constitution's own guidance is that repeated bad verdicts from one checker usually mean the clause is wrong. Two of this round's five failures — C-6's acknowledgement location and C-9's extraction breadth — are exactly that shape: a procedure stated one notch off, in a clause whose judgment is sound. The countermeasure is not more prose. It is naming the skill's own artifact as the procedure wherever one exists, which is what I have recommended for both: SKILL.md:122 decides C-6, lint-scope.sh:218-230 decides C-9. Neither costs a sentence more than the wrong version did. | Judgment-routed clauses: .agent-guild/state/constitution.md:19, :26, :33, :40, :47, :54, :61, :68, :75, :89, :96 (eleven judgment checks against two script checks at :12 and :82). - **C-1** (major): FAIL, and this is a clause r0, r1, and r2 all passed. The finding comes out of the hand-off question you asked me to verify. C-9's third exemption now reads '_maintenance/inbox-to-memory/EVALS.md itself (C-1)', which is an improvement on r2's unowned 'paths under _maintenance/inbox-to-memory/' — but C-1 does not check that name. Its check passes a directory prefix, _maintenance/inbox-to-memory/, and check-diff-scope.py treats a trailing-slash argument as 'anything under this prefix' (allowed_dirs at :147, prefix match at :114-116). So a deliverable written to _maintenance/inbox-to-memory/EVAL.md, or evals.md, or EVALS.markdown, is in scope and C-1 exits 0, while C-9 has explicitly declined to look at it. The exact filename EVALS.md is therefore owned by no clause in the document. eval-scope.sh is not exposed the same way — C-10's check names it twice and executes it, so a script named stage-eval.sh fails C-10 — which is what makes the EVALS.md case a hand-off gap rather than a general one. The fix is mechanical and it also closes the ceiling-versus-floor note r1 and r2 each raised and you declined twice: pass the two files as exact paths rather than as a prefix. check-diff-scope.py already supports this (allowed_files at :146 is every argument not ending in '/'). The check becomes `.agent-guild/scripts/check-diff-scope.py _maintenance/inbox-to-memory/EVALS.md _maintenance/inbox-to-memory/eval-scope.sh tests/fixtures/inbox-to-memory/evals/`, which is what the clause's own first sentence says ('The suite is exactly three things') and which fails a misnamed or a third file under that directory. It still does not verify the three exist, and I am not asking for that here — the floor is genuinely carried by C-2, C-3, and C-10 — but the clause should say so in one sentence instead of leaving a checker to read a green C-1 as having confirmed existence.

The revision closes r2's three-round residual squarely: keying the slice to the enumeration of scenario headings rather than to 'the next heading' means a `#### Expected` subheading no longer ends the slice early, and per-number reporting kills the 'five of six is passing' summary. But 'extract only the text between heading N and heading N+1' is undefined for the last scenario, because there is no heading N+1. A checker has to improvise the terminal boundary, and the two natural improvisations differ: end at `## Grading`, or run to end of file. Under the second, the last scenario's slice absorbs the Grading section — and C-12 requires that section to ship a results table with a row or column per scenario. Fix, four words: 'between heading N and heading N+1, or for the last scenario, the next `##` heading'.

- **C-7** (blocker): FAIL, but the mechanism you were least confident in is sound — I want to separate those two findings clearly, since you asked. On reproducibility: the two-stage resolution is reproducible, and I would not weaken it. Collecting signals is a bounded read of nine rows against one inbox file, eight of which are decidable off the file itself; narrowest-wins is a total order over three tiers, so two checkers who agree on the signal set cannot disagree on the resolution. On r2's findings (1) and (2), both closed: naming Conflict Resolution at :21-25 supplies the rule the table alone cannot supply for a multi-signal input, and 'Carrying a broader-tier signal is not itself a failure — the tiebreak case is built that way on purpose' replaces the flat rule that contradicted the mandated case. The tiebreak case and the ordinary project and client cases now pass the same check: project with {project, client} resolves to project; client with {client, journal} resolves to client. The journal case is where it breaks. Journal is the broadest tier, so under 'a multi-signal input must expect the narrowest tier among the signals present', a journal-expecting scenario can only pass if every signal it carries is a journal signal — a single-tier input. The text meanwhile requires all three cases to run on 'an input that could plausibly have gone elsewhere'. The check never tests that phrase, which leaves exactly two readings and a defect under each. Read the check alone and the plausibility requirement is unenforced for all three scenarios, so a project scenario carrying one project signal and nothing else — the trivial case the phrase exists to exclude — passes; that is a vacuity hole in the clause's own anti-triviality requirement. Read the text alongside it, with 'gone elsewhere' meaning 'carries another tier's signal', and the journal scenario is unsatisfiable: any narrower signal you add to make it non-trivial changes the correct answer away from journal. Two checkers will split on the journal scenario specifically, which is the same failure shape r2 diagnosed one scenario over. Fix: resolve the phrase in the check rather than leaving it to inference. Something like — 'Plausibility is graded on subject matter, not on signal count: an input must be one a careful reader could have mis-tiered. Because narrowest-wins makes journal unreachable from any input carrying a project or client signal, the journal case satisfies this on subject matter alone and must not be failed for carrying only journal signals.' Second, smaller, and I am overturning r2's severity on it rather than its substance: r2 wanted the recurrence layout rewritten to the grep's own shape `<client-root>/{pursuits,projects}/<project>/notes/`. The clause's 'in distinct project directories' does resolve correctly against the skill, because SKILL.md:33 defines a project directory as one sitting under `pursuits/<name>/` or `projects/<name>/`, and scope-decisions.md:35 uses the same phrase the clause borrows. This is a note, not a defect, and I would not spend an edit on it.

- **over-specification** (minor): Answering the question you asked beyond pass or fail: yes, two clauses now carry machinery heavier than the failure they prevent, and the pattern is worth naming because it is what three rounds of audit produce if nobody stops it. C-7 is the clear case. It asks a checker to run a nine-row signal extraction against three inbox files, resolve each through a documented tiebreak, and separately verify a multi-project directory layout behind one non-textual signal. That is more procedure than the four other fixture clauses combined, for a deliverable that is a markdown table of expected tokens. The failure it prevents — a scenario expecting the wrong tier — is real, but the cheap version of the check catches it: 'read the inbox file, state which tier the reference's table and its narrowest-wins rule select, and compare to the expected token.' The row-by-row collection is what makes it feel rigorous and is not what makes it correct. If you keep the machinery, keep it because the tiebreak case genuinely needs it, and say so; do not add a fourth stage. C-10 is the milder case: four conjuncts where three do the work, and the one that does not ('writes nothing outside the scratch directory') is the one a checker has no instrument for. The broader observation, offered as the thing I would actually watch in Phase 2: eight of thirteen clauses now route to checker-judgment, and five of those require the checker to execute something — run a migrator, diff two trees, grep a fixture tree, run three smoke suites, load a rubric. A judgment checker that has to be right about a procedure before it can be right about a judgment fails in a way that reads as a bad verdict, and the constitution's own guidance is that repeated bad verdicts from one checker usually mean the clause is wrong. Two of this round's five failures — C-6's acknowledgement location and C-9's extraction breadth — are exactly that shape: a procedure stated one notch off, in a clause whose judgment is sound. The countermeasure is not more prose. It is naming the skill's own artifact as the procedure wherever one exists, which is what I have recommended for both: SKILL.md:122 decides C-6, lint-scope.sh:218-230 decides C-9. Neither costs a sentence more than the wrong version did.
